title: IKI Ramen+Sushi
summary: Restaurant site built in Webflow, with scroll-triggered motion used to pace the menu sections instead of dumping the whole card on load.
description:
Jeffry Undiarto is a Master Sommelier who spent over a decade in fine dining, including a run at the two-Michelin-starred n/naka, before building IKI Hospitality around a few distinct Japanese concepts. **IKI Ramen+Sushi — ramen, sushi, and omakase across Hollywood and Koreatown — and AKAMI, a sushi-and-omakase-only concept in Toluca Lake and Arcadia, needed sites that felt like family without feeling identical.**

The answer was one shared component system — hero video module, omakase menu cards, per-location reservation blocks, gallery grid, chef bio section — built once and tuned per brand. The copy, imagery, and omakase structure change from site to site; the underlying system doesn't, which is what makes adding a third or fourth location mostly a content job, not a rebuild.
caseSub: IKI Hospitality runs a handful of modern Japanese concepts across LA under chef Jeffry Undiarto. **IKI Ramen+Sushi and AKAMI needed sites that read as siblings, not clones — the same underlying component system, tuned differently for a ramen-and-sushi flagship versus an omakase-only sushi bar.** Four locations, two brands, one build.

decisionsSub: Four calls that shaped the build more than any single line of code.

decisions.title: One system, not two designs
decisions.body: IKI and AKAMI could have been two unrelated builds. Instead the hero, omakase cards, reservation blocks, and gallery grid all come from one shared component set — so the two sites feel related without feeling identical.

decisions.title: Content model over hard-coding
decisions.body: IKI runs one connected omakase tasting; AKAMI runs two separate tiers. Rather than fork the template, the CMS structure was built loose enough to hold both shapes from day one.

decisions.title: Reservations as a plug-in
decisions.body: Four locations, four OpenTable experiences. One reservation component takes a location ID and does the rest — adding a fifth location is a data entry, not a design decision.

decisions.title: Consistency where it's invisible
decisions.body: Online ordering, hours, and location details live in the exact same place across both sites. Guests never notice this — which is the point.
